entities.summary:
Ulfilas (Ancient Greek: Οὐλφίλας; c. 311 – 383), known also as Wulfila(s) or Urphilas, was a 4th-century Gothic preacher of Cappadocian Greek descent who played a pivotal role in shaping the Gothic people's religious and cultural identity. Born around 311 CE, Ulfilas is believed to have been a native of the Roman province of Dacia, located in modern-day Romania. He was a key figure in the Gothic conversion to Christianity, which was facilitated by his translation of the Bible into the Gothic language.

Ulfilas's most notable achievement was the creation of the Gothic alphabet, which allowed the Gothic people to write their language for the first time. This innovation enabled the spread of Christianity among the Goths and other Germanic tribes, contributing significantly to the transformation of the cultural and religious landscape of Europe during the 4th and 5th centuries CE. The influence of Ulfilas can be seen in the subsequent development of the Gothic language and the spread of Christianity throughout Northern Europe.

Ulfilas's significance extends beyond his linguistic and religious contributions, as his actions helped to bridge the cultural divide between the Goths and the Roman Empire, facilitating a period of relative peace and cultural exchange between the two entities. This, in turn, had far-reaching consequences for the development of Christianity in Europe and the eventual rise of the Eastern Roman Empire.

The legacy of Ulfilas can be seen in the many churches and monasteries that were built in the 4th and 5th centuries CE, particularly in the region of modern-day Romania and Bulgaria. The influence of Ulfilas's translation of the Bible into the Gothic language can also be seen in the many Gothic inscriptions that have been discovered in this region.
